title: Planning and organisation across a term
introHtml:
The goal is to never fall more than a few days behind, because in any cumulative course a backlog grows faster than it can be cleared. A fixed weekly rhythm does most of the work. This holds for a school term, a university semester, a school year, or a self-study project such as a language or a professional certification.

Why backlogs are so dangerous: new material usually builds on old material. If you are three lessons behind in calculus, statistics or anatomy, today's lesson makes less sense, so it takes longer to learn, so you fall further behind. Debt in learning compounds like debt with interest. Planning is mostly about keeping that interest from ever starting.

items.title: The lifecycle of one lesson, lecture or chapter
items.leadHtml:
Every unit of new material (a lecture, a school lesson, a textbook chapter, a week of a language course, a module of an online course) goes through the same six steps. Most of the time cost sits in steps 3 to 5, and they are also where most of the learning happens.

  1. Before (10 to 15 min): skim or pretest. Skim the headings, figures and learning objectives, or try two or three questions on the topic before you study it. Why: your brain listens better when it already has hooks to hang things on and questions it wants answered. Getting a pretest question wrong is useful: it primes you to notice the answer when it comes. Example: before a history lecture on the causes of the First World War, write down the three causes you would guess. During the lecture you will notice which ones you missed.
  2. During: attend actively. Annotate the slides or your notes, and mark anything that confuses you with a "?" so you can find it later. Why: marking confusion in the moment costs a second and saves twenty minutes of hunting later. Passive listening feels like learning but leaves little behind. Example: in a programming class, write "? why does this loop stop at n-1" next to the code instead of trying to work it out while the teacher moves on.
  3. Same day (20 to 30 min): blank-page recall, then fill gaps. Close everything, write or sketch what you remember, then open the source and fill the gaps in another colour. Clear up the "?" marks with the textbook or a short video. Why: forgetting is steepest in the first day. One effortful recall on the same day roughly resets the forgetting curve and tells you exactly what you did not understand while the lesson is still fresh. Example: after an economics lecture on elasticity, you can draw the demand curve but cannot explain why luxury goods are more elastic. That gap is your next 10 minutes.
  4. Within 24 hours: make or select flashcards. Turn the facts that have no logic of their own (dates, vocabulary, formulas, names) into a few cards, or switch on the matching cards in a premade deck. Why: cards made while the material is fresh are better cards, and the spacing schedule starts on day one instead of the week before the exam. Example: after a Spanish lesson on the preterite, make 5 cloze cards for irregular forms ("ayer yo ___ (ir) al cine" → fui).
  5. Following days: spaced reviews. Cards daily; a quick blank-page recall of the whole topic on about day 3, 7, 14 and 30. Why: each review comes just as the memory starts to fade, which is when recalling it does the most good. A review takes far less time than relearning from zero. Example: a 5-minute recall of last week's chemistry topic on the bus is worth more than an hour of rereading it the night before the test.
  6. Weekly: mixed practice questions. Do questions that mix this week's topics with older ones. Why: mixing forces you to recognise which idea a problem needs, which is exactly what exams and real life ask. It also keeps old topics alive. Example: a physics set with two momentum problems, two energy problems and one from last month's kinematics, in random order.

parts.time: For one hour-long lecture or one textbook chapter, the extra work around it is roughly 60 to 90 minutes spread over a month: about 15 min before, 25 min the same day, 15 min of cards, and a few short reviews. That sounds like a lot, but it replaces most of the cramming you would otherwise do later. In terms of the scale used in this compendium, the daily backbone (recall questions, cards) costs ~0.5-1× per item, and the expensive extras are kept for the hard ideas.

items.title: Semester map
items.leadHtml: At the start, list every course, exam date and assessment in one calendar. Count back from each exam.

parts.why: Most deadline crises are not surprises; they are things that were visible in week one but never put next to each other. Seeing all deadlines on one page shows the collisions in advance: three essays due in the same week, or an exam the day after a project deadline. Counting back turns a distant date into a start date.
parts.how:
1. Collect every syllabus, course page or exam timetable.
  2. Put every exam, deadline, presentation and lab report in one calendar (paper wall planner or digital).
  3. For each big item, count back and mark a "start by" date and a "first draft" or "first full mock" date.
  4. Shade the crunch weeks so you can protect them (no extra shifts, no trips).

examples.simple: a secondary school student writes all end-of-term test dates on a wall calendar and sees that maths and biology fall on the same Monday, so biology revision starts a week earlier.
examples.nontrivial: a part-time MBA student working full time maps the term and sees that the corporate finance case and a busy work quarter-end collide. She books two days of annual leave in that week, before anyone else books them.

items.title: Weekly plan
items.leadHtml: Once a week (for example Sunday, about 20 minutes), look at the week's lessons, due reviews and deadlines. Block study time in the calendar like appointments.

parts.why: A week is the right size: big enough to balance subjects, small enough to predict. People are much better at estimating time when they break a job into concrete parts (Kruger & Evans 2004), and a weekly plan is exactly that. It also moves decisions out of the moment: on Tuesday at 6 pm you do not have to decide what to study, only to follow the plan.
parts.how:
1. Look at the semester map: what is due in the next two weeks?
  2. List the week's fixed events: classes, work, sport, family.
  3. Put reviews in first (they are not optional), then new material, then assignments.
  4. Leave white space; plan about 70 to 80% of your free time, not 100%.

examples.simple: a first-year law student blocks Monday and Wednesday evenings for contract law reading and Thursday morning for a practice problem.
examples.nontrivial: a nurse studying for a certification on rotating shifts plans her study blocks only after the roster is out, and puts the hardest topic on the day after a day off, not after a night shift.
examples.html:
• Simple: a first-year law student blocks Monday and Wednesday evenings for contract law reading and Thursday morning for a practice problem.
  • Non-trivial: a nurse studying for a certification on rotating shifts plans her study blocks only after the roster is out, and puts the hardest topic on the day after a day off, not after a night shift.

parts.time: About 20 minutes a week. It usually pays for itself on the first day.

items.title: Daily plan
items.leadHtml: Spend about 5 minutes picking 1 to 3 must-do tasks for the day. Everything else is a bonus.

parts.why: A long to-do list mixes the important with the trivial, and the trivial items are easier, so they win. Choosing a small number of must-dos makes success possible every day, which matters for motivation. Writing down a specific plan also quiets the mental nagging of unfinished goals (Masicampo & Baumeister 2011), so you can focus on the task in front of you.
parts.how:
1. Look at today's calendar block and the weekly plan.
  2. Write 1 to 3 tasks that would make the day a success. Make them concrete ("blank-page recall of lecture 6", not "study biochem").
  3. Do the first one before email, messages or anything else, if you can.

examples.simple: "1. Anki reviews. 2. Recall today's history lesson. 3. Finish question 4 of the problem sheet."
examples.nontrivial: a developer preparing for a cloud certification on a heavy work day writes only one must-do ("20 practice questions on networking at lunch") and treats anything more as a bonus. A small win on a bad day keeps the streak alive.

items.title: Time blocking
items.leadHtml: Fixed study blocks at the same times each day turn studying into a routine rather than a daily decision.

parts.why: Every decision ("should I study now? what first?") costs willpower and gives procrastination an opening. A block on the calendar is a decision made in advance. Cal Newport, who popularised the term, describes giving every hour of the work day a job and then adjusting the plan when reality changes, rather than abandoning it.
parts.how:
1. Find 2 to 4 times in your week that are reliably free and when you have energy.
  2. Give each block a label with a task ("19:00-20:30 Statistics: problem set 3").
  3. If something overruns, move the block; do not delete it.
  4. Use the same place and the same start ritual (water, phone in another room, timer) so starting becomes automatic.

examples.simple: a high school student does 30 minutes of French vocabulary every day straight after dinner.
examples.nontrivial: a music student blocks technical practice for the morning when her hands are fresh and theory homework for the evening, because the two use different kinds of energy. Matching the block to the energy matters as much as the time.
examples.html:
• Simple: a high school student does 30 minutes of French vocabulary every day straight after dinner.
  • Non-trivial: a music student blocks technical practice for the morning when her hands are fresh and theory homework for the evening, because the two use different kinds of energy. Matching the block to the energy matters as much as the time.

parts.watch: Blocks that are too long or too packed get broken and then abandoned. 60 to 90 minutes with a break is a good default.

items.title: Plan reviews before new material
items.leadHtml: Reviews first each day, then new content. Skipping reviews is how backlogs start.

parts.why: Reviews are small, due on a specific day, and get more expensive the longer you wait: a card reviewed on time takes 15 seconds, the same card forgotten takes several minutes to relearn. New material, by contrast, can wait a day without getting worse. If you do new material first, the reviews get squeezed out, then pile up, then feel overwhelming, and that is the compounding debt. Spaced reviews also give much better long-term retention for the same total time (Cepeda et al. 2006).
parts.how:
1. Start each study block with whatever reviews are due (cards, topic recall).
  2. Only then move to new lessons or assignments.
  3. If you are short on time, shrink new material, not reviews.

examples.simple: a language learner does her 15 minutes of Anki before opening the next textbook unit.
examples.nontrivial: an engineering student with 300 overdue cards after a holiday does not start new decks at all for three days. He works the overdue pile in 100-card batches, oldest topics first, and only then resumes new material. The backlog clears in under a week instead of growing.

items.title: A catch-up rule
items.leadHtml: If you fall behind, do not try to do everything. Do today's lessons first, then work the backlog in small chunks, highest-yield first.

parts.why: When you fall behind, the natural instinct is to go back to the oldest missed lecture and work forward. That keeps you permanently behind: you are always learning last week's material while this week's piles up. Staying current stops the debt growing; then you pay it off in instalments.
parts.how:
1. Keep up with today's and this week's material as if nothing were missing.
  2. List the backlog and rank it: what is most likely to be tested, and what do upcoming topics depend on?
  3. Add one or two small backlog chunks per day (one lecture, one chapter section).
  4. For low-yield items, a quick skim plus a few recall questions may be enough.

examples.simple: after a week off sick, a school student follows this week's maths lessons and catches up one missed lesson per evening.
examples.nontrivial: a medical student two weeks behind in pharmacology ranks the missed lectures by how often their drug classes appear in past papers. She fully catches up on the top four and covers the rest with flashcards only, accepting that a perfect catch-up is not possible.

items.title: Buffer days
items.leadHtml: Leave one lighter day per week for catch-up and rest.

parts.why: People consistently underestimate how long tasks will take, even when they know similar tasks overran before. This is the planning fallacy (Buehler, Griffin & Ross 1994). A plan with no slack breaks the first time something takes longer than expected, and a broken plan is often abandoned completely. A buffer absorbs the overrun so the rest of the week survives.
parts.how:
1. Mark one day (or two half-days) a week as "buffer": nothing new is scheduled.
  2. Use it first for anything that slipped, then for rest.
  3. If nothing slipped, the buffer is a reward, not a chance to cram more in.

examples.simple: Friday afternoon is the buffer: finish what slipped, then go out.
examples.nontrivial: a doctoral student writing a thesis chapter plans her estimates, then multiplies them by 1.5. Over three months her real times matched the inflated estimates far better than her original guesses, and she stopped missing supervisor deadlines.

items.title: Single capture system
items.leadHtml: Use one place for every task and deadline (a planner, a to-do app or a paper notebook). Nothing stays only in your head.

parts.why: An open loop (an unwritten task) keeps tugging at your attention, and it shows up at the worst moment, during study. David Allen's Getting Things Done method starts with "capture": collect everything that has your attention into one trusted inbox. Once your brain trusts the system to remember, it lets go. Having one place matters more than which app you use; two places means you trust neither.
parts.how:
1. Choose one tool and carry it always (phone app, pocket notebook).
  2. Write down every task, deadline and idea the moment it appears.
  3. Empty the inbox into your calendar or task list during the weekly plan.

examples.simple: a student writes "essay topic due Fri" in the notes app the moment the teacher says it, instead of "remembering" it.
examples.nontrivial: a self-taught programmer keeps a single text file with three headings: "to do", "to learn", "questions". Anything that would derail a focus session ("look up how Git rebase works") goes in it and gets sorted on Sunday.

items.title: Weekly review
items.leadHtml: Spend about 15 minutes on what got done, what slipped and what to change. This is where you adjust the method.

parts.why: Without feedback, a plan cannot improve; you just repeat the same mistakes with more guilt. The weekly review closes the loop: you compare your estimates with what happened (the direct cure for the planning fallacy), clear the capture inbox, and decide one change. parts.how:
Answer three questions in writing:

  1. What did I get done? (Done list, wins.)
  2. What slipped, and why? (Too ambitious, bad timing, distraction, illness?)
  3. What is one change for next week?

Then make next week's plan straight away, while the lessons are fresh.

examples.simple: "Got done: all reviews, 4 of 5 lectures. Slipped: essay outline, because Thursday evenings are always taken. Change: move essay block to Saturday morning."
examples.nontrivial: a language learner sees that her vocabulary scores rise but her speaking does not. She changes one block a week from cards to a 30-minute online conversation lesson, a change she would not have made without looking at the week as a whole.

items.bodyHtml:
Spend about 15 minutes on what got done, what slipped and what to change. This is where you adjust the method.

Why it works. Without feedback, a plan cannot improve; you just repeat the same mistakes with more guilt. The weekly review closes the loop: you compare your estimates with what happened (the direct cure for the planning fallacy), clear the capture inbox, and decide one change. David Allen calls the weekly review the critical success factor of his whole system.

How to do it. Answer three questions in writing:

  1. What did I get done? (Done list, wins.)
  2. What slipped, and why? (Too ambitious, bad timing, distraction, illness?)
  3. What is one change for next week?

Then make next week's plan straight away, while the lessons are fresh.

Examples.

  • Simple: "Got done: all reviews, 4 of 5 lectures. Slipped: essay outline, because Thursday evenings are always taken. Change: move essay block to Saturday morning."
  • Non-trivial: a language learner sees that her vocabulary scores rise but her speaking does not. She changes one block a week from cards to a 30-minute online conversation lesson, a change she would not have made without looking at the week as a whole.

items.title: Sample weeks
items.leadHtml:
Two very different lives, the same principles: reviews first, fixed blocks, a buffer, a weekly review.

Student A: university student, full-time, lectures in three courses.

DayMorningAfternoonEvening
MonLectures (stats, history)30 min same-day recall of both; cards45 min stats problem set
Tue20 min cards; pre-read biologyBiology lecture and labSame-day recall of biology; gym
WedLectures (stats, history)Recall; library block: history essay reading (90 min)Free
Thu20 min cardsBiology lecture; recall60 min mixed practice questions (all three courses)
FriLecture (history)Buffer: catch up on whatever slippedOff
SatEssay drafting (2 h)OffOff
SunOff20 min cardsWeekly review (15 min) and plan (20 min)

Student B: working adult, learning German for a B2 exam and a work certification on the side.

DayBefore work (30 min)Lunch (20 min)Evening
MonGerman cardsCertification practice questions45 min certification video module, then blank-page recall
TueGerman cardsGerman podcast with transcriptOnline German conversation lesson (45 min)
WedGerman cardsCertification questionsOff (family evening)
ThuGerman cardsGerman grammar exercises45 min certification module, then recall
FriGerman cardsFreeOff
Sat90 min: German writing practice, then mixed certification questionsBuffer
SunOffWeekly review and plan (20 min)

What they share: the cheap daily work (cards, short recall) happens every day, the expensive work (essays, modules, conversations) sits in a few protected blocks, and each week has one buffer and one review. Student B studies only about 7 to 8 hours a week, but because the work is spaced and retrieval-based, those hours go a long way.
